Wow, what an inaccurate title and crappy journalism. Parts of the article are quite misleading as well; it feels as if the author at best skimmed through the research paper and drew some conclusions out of thin air.

Some male players, however — the ones who were less-skilled at the game, and performing worse relative their peers — made frequent, nasty comments to the female gamers. In other words, sexist dudes are literally losers.

Nowhere in the actual paper does it say anything about "frequent, nasty comments". The voice communications they looked at were only labelled as "positive", "neutral", or "negative". There was nothing about frequency or nastiness.

Furthermore, it simply does not follow that "sexist dudes are literally losers". Nothing from the study denotes that the negative comments made towards the "female player" (quotes because it was just female voice recordings being played) were sexist in nature, and the fact that certain players made more negative comments towards the "female player" does not imply that they are maliciously or deliberately sexist. For example, maybe the players are more comfortable expressing their emotions towards a female player compared to a male player.

Finally, in no way can you take the data from the study and extrapolate to all "sexist dudes" or even all "dudes". The data was gathered in a single game, Halo 3, over 163 matches, and presumably over a short period of time around 2013. That would make Halo 3 about 6 years old, and I'm sure many of us are familiar with how quickly games, especially their multiplayer components, come and go over the course of a couple years, let alone 6 (Halo 3: ODST, Halo Reach, and possible Halo 4 came out between Halo 3's release and 2013).

Oh, and to top it all off, the article has a link to a GamerGate article (written by the same author), and that article starts off with a big picture of Anita Sarkeesian. So maybe take everything Caitlin Dewey writes with a truckload of salt.
